column2: And the old woman went up to the upper chamber, laughing aloud,
to tell her mistress that her dear husband was within;
and her knees were strengthened, and her feet stumbled with haste.
She stood above her head and spoke a word to her:

Wake, Penelope, dear child, that you may see
6	with your own eyes what you have longed for every day.
7	Odysseus has come and reached his house, though he came late.
8	And he has killed the proud suitors, who troubled his house
9	and ate his possessions and did violence to his son.
Then wise Penelope spoke to her in turn:

Dear nurse, the gods have made you mad, who are able
12	to make witless even one very sensible,
13	and who set the light-minded in the way of prudence;
14	they have harmed you; before you were sound in mind.
15	Why do you mock me, who have a sorrow-laden heart,
16	telling such things beside the mark, and wake me from sweet
17	sleep, which bound me, covering my dear eyelids?
18	For I have never slept so, since Odysseus
19	went off to see Ill-Ilium, not to be named.
20	But come now, go down and go back to the hall.
21	For if any other of the women who are mine
22	had come and told me this and woke me from sleep,
23	I would soon have sent her away in disgrace
24	back inside the hall; but this old age of yours will help you.
Then her dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to her in turn:

I do not mock you, dear child, but truly
27	Odysseus has come and reached his house, as I say,
28	the stranger, whom all dishonoured in the halls.
29	Telemachus long ago knew that he was within,
30	but with prudence he hid his father's plans,
31	that he might punish the violence of the overbearing men.
So she spoke, and she rejoiced, and leaping from her bed
she embraced the old woman, and let tears fall from her eyelids;
and speaking to her she addressed her with winged words:

Come now, dear nurse, tell me truly,
36	if indeed he has come to the house, as you say,
37	how he laid hands on the shameless suitors,
38	being alone, while they always remained together inside.
Then her dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to her in turn:

I did not see, I did not learn, but I heard only the groaning
41	of men being killed; and we in the innermost part of the well-built chambers
42	sat terrified, and well-fitted planks held the doors,
43	until your son called me from the hall,
44	Telemachus; for his father sent him to call me.
45	Then I found Odysseus among the slain corpses
46	standing; and around him, covering the hard ground,
47	they lay one upon another; you would have been cheered in heart to see.
48	And now they are all at the courtyard doors
50	in a heap, and he is purifying the very beautiful house
51	with a great fire he has kindled; and he sent me to call you.
52	But follow, that you both may enter on joy
53	in your dear hearts, since you have suffered many evils.
54	And now this long-cherished wish has been fulfilled;
55	he has come himself alive to his hearth, and found you
56	and his son in the halls; and those suitors who treated him ill,
57	all of them he has punished in his own house.
Then wise Penelope spoke to her in turn:

Dear nurse, do not yet boast loudly, laughing aloud.
60	For you know how welcome he would appear in the halls
61	to all, and above all to me and the son whom we begot;
62	but this story is not true, as you say,
63	but one of the immortals killed the noble suitors,
64	angered at their heart-grieving insolence and evil deeds.
65	For they honoured no one of men upon the earth,
66	neither bad nor good, whoever came to them;
67	therefore through their wantonness they suffered evil; but Odysseus
68	has lost far away his homecoming to the Achaean land, and himself perished.
Then her dear nurse Eurycleia answered her:

My child, what word has escaped the fence of your teeth,
71	you who said that your husband, who is inside by the hearth, would never
72	come home; your heart is always unbelieving.
73	But come, I shall tell you another clear sign,
74	the scar, which once a boar struck him with a white tusk.
75	This I noticed as I washed him, and I wanted to tell
76	you yourself; but he, seizing me by the mouth with his hands,
77	did not let me speak, in the great cunning of his mind.
78	But follow; and I will stake my own self on it;
79	if I deceive you, kill me by the most piteous death.
Then wise Penelope answered her:

Dear nurse, it is hard for you to grasp the designs
82	of the gods who live for ever, however wise you are.
83	But all the same let us go to my son, that I may see
84	the suitors dead, and him who killed them.
So saying she came down from the upper chamber; and much her heart
pondered, whether to question her dear husband from afar,
or to go up, and kiss his head, taking his hands.
But when she came in and crossed the stone threshold,
she sat opposite Odysseus, in the light of the fire,
by the other wall; and he was sitting by the tall pillar
looking down, waiting to see if she would say anything to him,
his mighty wife, when she saw him with her eyes.
But she sat long in silence, and wonder came upon her heart;
now she would look at him face to face,
now she would fail to know him, wearing bad clothes on his body.
And Telemachus rebuked her, and spoke a word and called by name:

My mother, unkind mother, with a hard heart,
98	why do you hold off thus from my father, and do not sit
99	beside him and ask him with words and enquire?
100	No other woman with an enduring heart would thus
101	stand aloof from her husband, who after suffering many evils
102	came in the twentieth year to his native land;
103	but your heart is always harder than stone.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

My child, my spirit is amazed in my breast,
106	and I cannot say a word, nor ask anything,
107	nor look him in the face. But if truly
108	this is Odysseus and he has come home, surely we two
109	shall know each other, and better; for we have
110	signs, which we two also know, hidden from others.
So she spoke, and the much-enduring godly Odysseus smiled,
and at once addressed Telemachus with winged words:

Telemachus, leave your mother in the halls
114	to test me; she will soon see better.
115	But now because I am dirty, and wear bad clothes on my body,
116	therefore she dishonours me and says I am not he.
117	But let us consider how things may turn out best.
118	For even one who has killed a single man in the district,
119	who does not have many avengers behind him,
120	flees, leaving kinsmen and his native land;
121	but we have killed the bulwark of the city, who were by far the best
122	of the youths in Ithaca; this I bid you consider.
Then prudent Telemachus answered him:

See to that yourself, dear father; for your counsel they say is the best
125	among men, and no other man
126	among mortal men could contend with you.
127	And we shall follow eagerly with you, and I say we shall not
128	fall short in valour, so far as our strength is there.
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Therefore I will say what seems to me best.
131	First wash and put on tunics,
132	and bid the maidservants in the halls take their clothes;
133	and let the godly singer, holding the clear-toned lyre,
134	lead us in a playful dance,
135	so that anyone hearing outside would say it is a wedding,
136	either walking on the road, or those who live around;
137	lest wide report of the slaughter of the suitors
138	spread through the town, before we have gone out
139	to our much-wooded farm; and there afterwards
140	we shall consider what advantage the Olympian may put in our hands.
So he spoke, and they heard him well and obeyed.
First then they washed and put on tunics,
and the women dressed themselves; and the godly singer took
the hollow lyre, and roused in them the desire
for sweet song and blameless dance.
And the great house resounded about them with the feet
of men dancing and fair-girdled women.
And thus one would say, hearing from outside the house:
So someone said, and they did not know how it had been done.
But great-hearted Odysseus in his own house
Eurynome the housekeeper bathed and anointed with oil,
and threw about him a fair cloak and a tunic;
and on his head Athena poured much beauty,
making him taller to look at and stouter; and from his head
she made the curly hair fall, like the hyacinth flower.
As when a man pours gold over silver,
a skilled man, whom Hephaestus and Pallas Athena have taught
art of every kind, and he finishes graceful works;
so she poured grace over his head and shoulders.
And he came out of the bath, in form like the immortals;
and sat down again on the chair from which he had risen,
opposite his wife, and spoke a word to her:

Strange woman, beyond all womankind
167	the dwellers of Olympus have made your heart unyielding;
168	no other woman with an enduring heart would thus
169	stand aloof from her husband, who after suffering many evils
170	came in the twentieth year to his native land.
171	But come, nurse, spread me a bed, that I too myself
172	may lie down; for she has an iron heart in her breast.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

Strange man, I neither think highly nor slight you,
175	nor am I overly amazed, and I know well what you were like
176	when you went from Ithaca on the long-oared ship.
177	But come, spread for him the sturdy bed, Eurycleia,
178	outside the well-built chamber, which he himself made;
179	bring it out there and put on it the bedding,
180	fleeces and cloaks and shining rugs.
So she spoke, testing her husband; but Odysseus,
vexed, spoke to his wife who knew kindly things:

O woman, truly this is a heart-grieving word you have spoken.
184	Who has put my bed elsewhere? It would be hard
185	even for one very skilled, unless a god himself came
186	and easily, if he wished, set it in another place.
187	But of men no living mortal, not even in the prime of youth,
188	could easily move it, since a great sign is wrought
189	in the carefully made bed; I built it and no one else.
190	A bush of long-leaved olive grew inside the court,
191	vigorous, flourishing; its trunk was thick as a pillar.
192	Around it I built the chamber, until I finished it,
193	with close-set stones, and roofed it well above,
194	and set on it jointed doors, closely fitted.
195	And then I cut off the foliage of the long-leaved olive,
196	and trimming the trunk from the root I smoothed it round with bronze
197	well and skilfully, and made it straight to the line,
198	fashioning a bed-post, and bored it all with an auger.
199	Beginning from this I polished the bed, until I finished it,
200	adorning it with gold and silver and ivory;
201	and I stretched on it a thong of ox-hide, shining with purple.
202	So I declare this sign to you; and I do not know,
203	woman, whether my bed is still firm, or whether some man
204	has already put it elsewhere, cutting under the root of the olive.
So he spoke, and her knees and dear heart were loosened on the spot,
as she recognised the signs that Odysseus told her unerringly;
then weeping she ran straight to him, and around
Odysseus' neck threw her hands, and kissed his head, and said:

Do not be angry with me, Odysseus, since in other things above all
210	men you are wise; the gods gave us misery,
211	who begrudged that we two, staying beside each other,
212	should enjoy our youth and come to the threshold of old age.
213	But do not now be angry at this or blame me,
214	because I did not welcome you thus at first, when I saw you.
215	For always the heart in my dear breast
216	shuddered lest some mortal come and deceive me with words;
217	for many devise evil gains.
218	Not even Argive Helen, born of Zeus,
219	would have lain in love and bed with a foreign man,
220	if she had known that the warlike sons of the Achaeans would
221	bring her back home to her dear native land.
222	But a god roused her to do the shameful deed;
223	and she did not before lay in her heart the baneful
224	folly, from which first grief came to us too.
225	But now, since you have told the clear signs
226	of our bed, which no other mortal has seen,
227	but only you and I and one single handmaid,
228	Actoris, whom my father gave me when I came here,
229	who kept the doors of our strong chamber,
230	you persuade my heart, however hard it is.
So she spoke, and in him she roused still more desire for lament;
and he wept, holding his beloved wife, who knew kindly things.
As when land appears welcome to swimmers,
whose well-built ship Poseidon on the sea
has shattered, driven by wind and heavy wave;
few escape from the grey sea to the land
swimming, and much brine is caked on their skin,
and welcome they set foot on land, escaping evil;
so welcome to her was her husband as she looked at him,
and from his neck she did not yet wholly let go her white arms.
And they would have wept until rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
had not the goddess grey-eyed Athena thought of something else.
The long night she held back at its end, and Dawn
she kept at Oceanus, golden-throned, and did not let her yoke
the swift-footed horses, bringers of light to men,
Lampus and Phaethon, the colts which draw Dawn.
And then Odysseus of many wiles spoke to his wife:

O woman, we have not yet come to the end of all
249	our trials, but still behind there will be measureless toil,
250	much and hard, which I must accomplish all.
251	For so the spirit of Teiresias prophesied to me
252	on that day when I went down into the house of Hades,
253	seeking a homecoming for my comrades and myself.
254	But come, let us go to bed, woman, that now at once
255	we may take our fill of sweet sleep, lying down.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

Your bed will be yours whenever your spirit
258	wishes, since the gods have made you reach
259	your well-built house and your native land.
260	But since you have thought of it and a god has put it in your mind,
261	come, tell me the contest, since I think I shall learn it later,
262	and to know it at once is no worse.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Strange woman, why now, urging me so much, do you bid me
265	tell? But I will tell and not hide it.
266	Your heart will not rejoice; nor do I myself
267	rejoice, since he bade me go to very many cities
268	of mortals, holding in my hands a well-shaped oar,
269	until I come to men who know not the sea,
270	nor eat food mixed with salt;
271	nor indeed do they know ships with crimson cheeks,
272	nor well-shaped oars, which are the wings of ships.
273	And he told me this clear sign, and I will not hide it from you:
274	when another traveller meeting me
275	says I have a winnowing-fan on my shining shoulder,
276	then he bade me fix my oar in the ground,
277	and offer fair sacrifices to lord Poseidon,
278	a ram and a bull and a boar, mounter of sows,
279	and depart home, and offer holy hecatombs
280	to the immortal gods who hold the broad heaven,
281	to all, one after another; and death for me from the sea itself
282	very gentle shall come, which shall kill me
283	worn out with sleek old age; and around me the peoples
284	will be prosperous; this he said would all be fulfilled for me.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

If indeed the gods will bring a better old age,
287	there is hope then that there will be an escape from evils.
So they spoke such things to one another;
and meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse prepared the bed
with soft covering, under blazing torches.
And when they had spread the sturdy bed, hurrying,
the old woman went back to the house to lie down,
and Eurynome the chamber-attendant led them
as they went to the bed, holding a torch in her hands;
and having led them to the chamber she went back. And they then
gladly came to the rites of their old bed.
But Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
stopped the feet from dancing, and stopped the women,
and themselves lay down in the shadowy halls.
And the two, when they had taken their fill of lovely love,
took pleasure in telling stories, speaking to each other,
she, the divine one among women, of all she had endured in the halls,
looking on the destructive crowd of suitors,
who for her sake had slaughtered many, oxen and fat sheep,
and much wine was drawn from the jars;
and Zeus-born Odysseus told what troubles he had brought
on men, and all he himself had toiled through in suffering;
all he told; and she was delighted listening, and sleep
did not fall on her eyelids before he had told it all.
He began with how first he subdued the Cicones, and then
came to the rich land of the Lotus-eaters;
and all the Cyclops did, and how he paid back the penalty
for his mighty comrades, whom he ate and did not pity;
and how he came to Aeolus, who received him with ready goodwill
and sent him on, but it was not yet his fate to reach
his dear native land, but a storm wind snatching him again
carried him over the fishy sea, groaning heavily;
and how he came to Telepylus of the Laestrygonians,
who destroyed the ships and all his well-greaved
comrades; and Odysseus alone escaped in his black ship;
and he told of Circe's guile and her many devices,
and how he went to the mouldy house of Hades,
to consult the spirit of Theban Teiresias,
in his many-benched ship, and saw all his comrades
and his mother, who bore him and nursed him when little;
and how he heard the voice of the clear-singing Sirens,
and how he came to the Wandering Rocks and dread Charybdis
and Scylla, whom never yet did men escape unharmed;
and how his comrades killed the cattle of Helios;
and how Zeus high-thundering struck his swift ship
with a smoking thunderbolt, and his good comrades perished
all alike, and he alone escaped evil fates;
and how he came to the island Ogygia and the nymph Calypso,
who kept him back, longing for him to be her husband,
in her hollow caves, and nourished him and said
she would make him immortal and ageless all his days;
but she never persuaded the spirit in his breast;
and how he came to the Phaeacians after much toil,
who honoured him greatly in their heart like a god
and sent him with a ship to his dear native land,
giving him bronze and gold in plenty and clothing.
This was the last word he spoke, when sweet sleep
limb-loosening rushed on him, loosing the cares of his heart.
And the goddess grey-eyed Athena thought of other things:
when she hoped that Odysseus in his heart
had had his fill of love with his wife and of sleep,
at once from Oceanus she roused golden-throned early-born Dawn,
to bring light to men; and Odysseus rose
from his soft bed, and gave charge to his wife:

O woman, already we have had our fill of many trials,
351	we both, you here weeping for my troublous return,
352	and me Zeus and the other gods with pains
353	held back, eager as I was, from my native land;
354	but now that we both have come to our much-desired bed,
355	the possessions that are mine, take care of in the halls,
356	and the flocks which the overweening suitors wasted,
357	many I myself shall raid, and others the Achaeans
358	will give, until they fill all the folds.
359	But I shall go to the much-wooded farm,
360	to see my noble father, who is greatly grieved for me;
361	and to you, woman, I give this charge, wise though you are:
362	for at once with the rising sun a report will go
363	of the suitors whom I killed in the halls;
364	go up to the upper chamber with your women attendants
365	and sit, and look at no one nor ask anything.
He spoke, and put on his shoulders the fair armour,
and roused Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd,
and bade them all take their arms of war in their hands.
They did not disobey him, and armed themselves with bronze,
and opened the doors, and went out; and Odysseus led.
Now there was light on the earth, but Athena
hiding them in night led them quickly out of the city.
